title: First field assessment of the green lacewing Chrysoperla carnea (Neuroptera: Chrysopidae) as a biological control agent of Tuta absoluta (Lepidoptera: Gelechiidae) on tomato in Tajikistan
authors: Ismoilov KI, Jalilov AU, Han P, Vidal-Quist JC, Desneux N
design: Two experiments: (1) Cage exclusion experiment — 20 exclusion cages (2 × 2 × 2 m, nylon mesh) each containing 12–13 tomato plants; 3 treatments randomly assigned: pre-fruiting release of C. carnea (n = 7 cages), post-fruiting release of C. carnea (n = 7 cages), no release control (n = 6 cages). Pre-fruiting release: 500 C. carnea eggs per cage applied once at vegetative stage (mid-August). Post-fruiting release: 500 C. carnea eggs per cage applied once at fruiting stage (mid-September). (2) Open-field experiment — two 0.5 ha fields (~2500 plants each): biocontrol field (two inundative C. carnea egg releases, pre-fruiting + post-fruiting) vs control field (no release). Yield measured as total fruit weight per cage at season end (5–8 October 2018), converted to per-plant average. Season: August–October 2018.
notes: This is an ADDITION experiment: treatment = augmented arm (C. carnea released), control = no release (natural/ambient predator levels). Yield data available only from the cage experiment (Fig. 4). The open-field experiment produced no yield comparison because control-field plants were almost completely destroyed by T. absoluta around 20 September, preventing data collection (p. 8 text). Pest abundance data (feeding galleries, young larvae, old larvae per plant) reported only as repeated-measures time series across 7 sampling dates in Fig. 3a–c (cage) and Fig. 3d–f (open field), with no season-average or cumulative summary statistics. Chi-squared tests confirm significant treatment effects (feeding galleries: χ² = 200.6, df = 2, p < 0.001; young larvae: χ² = 114.5, df = 2, p < 0.001; old larvae: χ² = 125.2, df = 2, p < 0.001 for cage experiment). These time-series data are not extractable as single-value observations. For the open-field pest data, control data stops after 4 of 7 sampling dates (plants destroyed). The cage experiment n is asymmetric: 7 cages for each release treatment, 6 for control. ANOVA for yield: F(2,17) = 48.00, p < 0.001, confirming df_error = 17 consistent with 20 total cages. Variance in Fig. 4 is ± SE per caption.

observations.treatment_description: Pre-fruiting release — 500 C. carnea eggs released per exclusion cage once at the vegetative stage (mid-August 2018); cages covered with nylon mesh enclosing 12–13 tomato plants
observations.control_description: No release (control) — exclusion cages with no C. carnea release; natural ambient conditions inside mesh cage; 12–13 tomato plants per cage

figure_read.evidence_note: Fig 4 p8; leftmost bar (Pre-fruiting release, dark gray); bar top sits just below the 1.0 gridline, approximately 75% of the way from 0.8 to 1.0 tick → ~0.95 kg. Letter 'a' above. Error bar cap extends to about 1.05, SE ≈ 0.10. Control bar (rightmost, lightest): top at about 75% from 0.2 to 0.4 tick → ~0.35 kg. Direction: C. carnea release increases yield — consistent with expected biocontrol effect (addition experiment). n_control = 6 cages (vs n_treatment = 7).

observations.notes: Pre-fruiting C. carnea release nearly tripled yield compared to unprotected control. Both release timings showed letter 'a' (not significantly different from each other) but significantly higher than control (letter 'b'). ANOVA F(2,17) = 48.00, p < 0.001. SE for treatment read from error bar cap at ~1.05 minus bar top at 0.95 = 0.10. n_control = 6 cages, n_treatment = 7 cages.
